Texas Instruments and Lam Research Report Earnings: AI Equipment Boom Meets Analog Rebound
Lam Research and Texas Instruments both report after the close on Wednesday, and each faces a different kind of pressure: one must prove AI equipment demand is still accelerating, while the other needs to show its industrial recovery has real…
Published October 20, 2026, 7:50am ET · 3 min read
Automated robotic arms meticulously assemble electronic components on an advanced manufacturing line, illustrating the high-tech production methods driving growth in the semiconductor industry, particularly for AI equipment and industrial applications. © Shutterstock
Two chip stocks from opposite ends of the industry report on Wednesday, October 21, after the market close. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX | LRCX Price Prediction) has to show that AI equipment demand is still accelerating. Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) has to show that its industrial and auto rebound can last.
Texas Instruments hosts its call at 3:30 p.m. Central time (4:30 p.m. ET). Lam follows at 5:00 p.m. ET.
Texas Instruments Faces a Test of Its Own Guidance
Texas Instruments makes analog chips that handle real-world signals like power and temperature. It also makes embedded processors, the small control chips built into machines. On its prior earnings call, Texas Instruments said revenue rose 13% sequentially and 23% year over year. Industrial, data center, and automotive customers led the growth.
Texas Instruments guided third-quarter revenue to $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and EPS to $2.23 to $2.57. The consensus EPS estimate of $2.42 falls inside that range, so the fourth-quarter outlook carries more weight. Management said industrial revenue remains below its 2022 peak and customer inventories have not been rebuilt. Auto demand picked up, led by electric vehicles and hybrids in China. Shares are up 59.2% year to date.
Lam Research Rides AI Demand Into Record Guidance
Lam sells deposition and etch tools, the machines that add and carve away thin layers of material on silicon wafers. On its prior earnings call, Lam said it delivered record revenue, operating margin, and earnings per share “as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry,” positioning it for “a third consecutive year of outperformance in 2026.”
Lam guided September-quarter revenue to $8.1 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and EPS to $2.15 plus or minus $0.15. It also raised its 2026 forecast for wafer fab equipment spending (what the whole industry spends on chipmaking tools) to the low $150 billion range.
In an August 26 Bloomberg Businessweek report, Lam Research said its advanced packaging business is growing more than 70% year over year. Advanced packaging stacks memory and processor chips in three dimensions and wires them together, so AI hardware works like one large system. Lam shares are down 12.1% over the past week and up 59.0% year to date.
Consensus Points to Steep Year-Over-Year Gains
Jim Cramer described the demand picture on October 19, saying CPUs are “going to be in very short supply, which I think is absolutely true because Taiwan Semi can’t make all the ones that they have.” He added, “There’s tremendous demand, and there’s also an inability to build.” On October 9, he said, “Taiwan Semi controlled pretty much any chip stock.”
When chipmakers cannot build fast enough, they add factory capacity, and that means buying more deposition and etch tools from Lam. Lam said the industry remains meaningfully undersupplied, with several new fabs expected to come online by the end of 2027. The same buildout is pulling in power, cooling, and networking suppliers alongside the chipmakers. (We rounded up seven of those names in a free AI infrastructure report.)
What Each Company Must Prove on Wednesday
Texas Instruments needs a fourth-quarter outlook showing that industrial and automotive demand is still climbing. Lam needs revenue close to its $8.1 billion guidance and more detail on 2027, a year management already called a potentially strong setup.

Here are highlights from Monday's Analyst Blog:
Q3 Earnings Reports Gear Up: Global Week Ahead
What happens across this Global Week Ahead?

Elsewhere:

Next are Reuters' five world market themes, re-ordered for equity traders—
U.S. earnings season picks up in the coming days, with investors focused on Meta Platforms and other AI-focused companies as technology shares wobble.
Meta, due on Wednesday, is one of several hyper-scalers whose massive spending on AI data centers and infrastructure has been a big driver of investment.
With concerns mounting over financing for the AI buildout, investors want more detail on expected returns from those huge outlays.
Reports from semiconductor companies Lam Research and Texas Instruments will offer another view of the AI boom, as will results from Elon Musk's Tesla.
Other high-profile results in the coming days include Netflix, Procter & Gamble and GE Aerospace.
S&P500 earnings are expected to have climbed more than +30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, continuing a robust year for corporate profits.
(2) Stock & Bond Returns Correlation a Focus
For months, as energy and food prices surged amid the Iran war, bonds lost their shock-absorber status as investors jacked up estimates of how high interest rates might need to go.
Add near-chronic concern ‌about developed-world governments' finances, and bonds seemed to offer little safe-haven comfort while still struggling to rival super-charged equities.
The correlation between stocks and bond yields has now turned positive for Europe and the U.S., meaning yields are more likely to fall when stocks fall.
It had been overwhelmingly negative this year, with yields rising as stocks fell, undermining bonds' traditional role as a haven during equity selloffs.
This relationship fluctuates, but this year, the correlation of U.S. stocks and bond yields in March hit its most negative since at least the 1990s, while for European assets, it reached its most negative on record in September.
(3) MSCI Proposed Stripping Indonesia of EM Status. Turkey Put on Notice, Too
Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey already have plenty on their plates.

Indonesia's central bank meets on Wednesday, while Turkish policymakers gather on Thursday, against a backdrop of high energy prices, rising borrowing costs, AI-driven market disruption and geopolitical uncertainty.

At a forward P/E of 27.55, TXN now trades higher than its forward multiples of 25.58 at the end of 2025 and 26.25 in September 2025, according to Yahoo Finance. That forward P/E means investors are getting an earnings yield of just 3.63%, not great when you compare it to the 5.2% yield you could get from a 10-year Treasury in mid-October. And while Treasury payouts are rock solid, Texas Instruments' profits can swing with the business cycle. The company could still deliver solid returns if it keeps growing earnings and raising the dividend, but the current price gives investors less cushion if things don't go as planned.
Looking at the competition, it's easy to see why a little caution is smart. Analog Devices, for example, traded at about 23.2 times forward earnings, well below Texas Instruments' 27.55. TXN's bigger scale and wide range of analog products might explain the higher price, but to keep that edge, the company will need to deliver more than just a return to normal demand. In September, TI announced it was bumping its quarterly dividend up by 7% to $1.52, or $6.08 per year. Based on the October 16 share price of $276.48, that's a forward yield of about 2.2%. TI's 23-year track record of raising its dividend and its growing cash flow make it appealing for income-focused investors. But with a payout ratio this high, there's not much room for earnings to slip without putting the dividend at risk. Big spending on factories and the ups and downs of industry demand are still key risks, especially if the recovery loses steam.
Texas Instruments brings real long-term strengths and a steadily rising dividend to the table, but today's valuation means it can't afford to stumble. With a forward earnings yield lower than Treasuries and a high payout ratio, the case for buying in now relies mainly on the company's ability to keep growing its profits and raising its dividend.

Shares of Texas Instruments (TXN) rose 60.4% in the twelve months to October 19, 2026, against 16.8% for the S&P 500. The stock posted its largest one-day gain in that time on April 23, 2026. It climbed 19.4% the day after the chip maker reported first-quarter results and forecast second-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates. So what changed inside Texas Instruments to earn that price?
Texas Instruments' Sales Growth Picked Up In 2026
Texas Instruments has issued four quarterly reports since last October. Sales growth slowed in the first two periods, from 16.4% in fiscal Q2 2025 to 14.2% in fiscal Q3 2025 and 10.4% in fiscal Q4 2025. Growth then picked up in the next two quarters. Revenue climbed 18.6% in fiscal Q1 2026, and rose 22.8% to $5.46 billion in fiscal Q2 2026.
Reuters tied both forecasts that came before the stock's biggest jumps to data centers. In January, the news agency linked a jump in the shares on January 28 to a first-quarter outlook that signaled robust AI data center demand. The stock closed 9.9% higher that day. Automated robotic arms meticulously assemble electronic components on an advanced manufacturing line, illustrating the high-tech production methods driving growth in the semiconductor industry, particularly for AI equipment and industrial applications. © Shutterstock
Two chip stocks from opposite ends of the industry report on Wednesday, October 21, after the market close. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX | LRCX Price Prediction) has to show that AI equipment demand is still accelerating. Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) has to show that its industrial and auto rebound can last.
Texas Instruments hosts its call at 3:30 p.m. Central time (4:30 p.m. ET). Lam follows at 5:00 p.m. ET.
Texas Instruments Faces a Test of Its Own Guidance
Texas Instruments makes analog chips that handle real-world signals like power and temperature. It also makes embedded processors, the small control chips built into machines. On its prior earnings call, Texas Instruments said revenue rose 13% sequentially and 23% year over year. Industrial, data center, and automotive customers led the growth.
Texas Instruments guided third-quarter revenue to $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and EPS to $2.23 to $2.57. The consensus EPS estimate of $2.42 falls inside that range, so the fourth-quarter outlook carries more weight. Management said industrial revenue remains below its 2022 peak and customer inventories have not been rebuilt. Auto demand picked up, led by electric vehicles and hybrids in China. Shares are up 59.2% year to date.
Lam Research Rides AI Demand Into Record Guidance
Lam sells deposition and etch tools, the machines that add and carve away thin layers of material on silicon wafers. On its prior earnings call, Lam said it delivered record revenue, operating margin, and earnings per share “as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry,” positioning it for “a third consecutive year of outperformance in 2026.”
Lam guided September-quarter revenue to $8.1 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and EPS to $2.15 plus or minus $0.15. It also raised its 2026 forecast for wafer fab equipment spending (what the whole industry spends on chipmaking tools) to the low $150 billion range.
In an August 26 Bloomberg Businessweek report, Lam Research said its advanced packaging business is growing more than 70% year over year. Advanced packaging stacks memory and processor chips in three dimensions and wires them together, so AI hardware works like one large system. Lam shares are down 12.1% over the past week and up 59.0% year to date.
Consensus Points to Steep Year-Over-Year Gains
Jim Cramer described the demand picture on October 19, saying CPUs are “going to be in very short supply, which I think is absolutely true because Taiwan Semi can’t make all the ones that they have.” He added, “There’s tremendous demand, and there’s also an inability to build.” On October 9, he said, “Taiwan Semi controlled pretty much any chip stock.”
When chipmakers cannot build fast enough, they add factory capacity, and that means buying more deposition and etch tools from Lam. Lam said the industry remains meaningfully undersupplied, with several new fabs expected to come online by the end of 2027. The same buildout is pulling in power, cooling, and networking suppliers alongside the chipmakers. (We rounded up seven of those names in a free AI infrastructure report.)
What Each Company Must Prove on Wednesday
Texas Instruments needs a fourth-quarter outlook showing that industrial and automotive demand is still climbing. Lam needs revenue close to its $8.1 billion guidance and more detail on 2027, a year management already called a potentially strong setup.

Here are highlights from Monday's Analyst Blog:
Q3 Earnings Reports Gear Up: Global Week Ahead
What happens across this Global Week Ahead?
· Q3 earnings season is shifting up a gear in the U.S., and
· Mainland China is about to deliver a deluge of macro data
· Giving febrile markets plenty more to ponder after the latest bouts of volatility in bonds and AI stocks
Elsewhere:
· Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey have been given headaches by global index provider MSCI, while
· Voters in Brazil gear up to choose their next president
Next are Reuters' five world market themes, re-ordered for equity traders—
U.S. earnings season picks up in the coming days, with investors focused on Meta Platforms and other AI-focused companies as technology shares wobble.
Meta, due on Wednesday, is one of several hyper-scalers whose massive spending on AI data centers and infrastructure has been a big driver of investment.
With concerns mounting over financing for the AI buildout, investors want more detail on expected returns from those huge outlays.
Reports from semiconductor companies Lam Research and Texas Instruments will offer another view of the AI boom, as will results from Elon Musk's Tesla.
Other high-profile results in the coming days include Netflix, Procter & Gamble and GE Aerospace.
S&P500 earnings are expected to have climbed more than +30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, continuing a robust year for corporate profits.
(2) Stock & Bond Returns Correlation a Focus
For months, as energy and food prices surged amid the Iran war, bonds lost their shock-absorber status as investors jacked up estimates of how high interest rates might need to go.
Add near-chronic concern ‌about developed-world governments' finances, and bonds seemed to offer little safe-haven comfort while still struggling to rival super-charged equities.
The correlation between stocks and bond yields has now turned positive for Europe and the U.S., meaning yields are more likely to fall when stocks fall.
It had been overwhelmingly negative this year, with yields rising as stocks fell, undermining bonds' traditional role as a haven during equity selloffs.
This relationship fluctuates, but this year, the correlation of U.S. stocks and bond yields in March hit its most negative since at least the 1990s, while for European assets, it reached its most negative on record in September.
(3) MSCI Proposed Stripping Indonesia of EM Status. Turkey Put on Notice, Too
Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey already have plenty on their plates.
Now they have an MSCI headache, too.
Indonesia's central bank meets on Wednesday, while Turkish policymakers gather on Thursday, against a backdrop of high energy prices, rising borrowing costs, AI-driven market disruption and geopolitical uncertainty.
MSCI has proposed stripping Indonesia of its emerging-market (EM) status and removing it from a suite of indexes, a move that risks triggering heavy outflows and raising pressure on policymakers to hike from 5.75% rather than hold.
MSCI has also put Turkey on notice, warning of a potential downgrade if market reforms fall short by mid-2027, another complication for policymakers expected to keep cutting rates from 37%.
(4) The Week Starts with a Mainland China Macro Data Deluge
A health check on the Chinese economy is due on Monday, with third-quarter GDP alongside September retail sales, industrial output and fixed-asset investment data.
The latest loan prime rate follows on Tuesday and is expected to stay put after more than a year on hold.
Strong global demand for semiconductors, clean technology and other manufactured goods has kept China's economy ticking, even as domestic demand remains patchy and higher energy costs bite.
Exports have held up despite China's delicate trade balancing act with the U.S. and E.U.
The latest trade figures showed Chinese exports surging well beyond analysts' estimates, putting the country on track for another $1 trillion trade surplus this year after crossing the threshold for the first time in 2025.
The flip side: the export boom could add to trade tensions with major partners.
(4) Brazil's Presidential Runoff Happens on October 25th. Campaigning Underway
Brazil's October 25th presidential runoff is keeping markets on edge after Flávio Bolsonaro's surprise first-round lead sent stocks up 7.7% and the real almost 4% higher.
A new Quaest poll puts Bolsonaro on 46% versus Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's 44%, a technical tie.
Investors are betting a Bolsonaro win would bring tighter fiscal policy, but much may already be priced in. His choice of economic team and signs of credible reform could fuel further gains.
A Lula comeback, meanwhile, could put that rally into reverse, with the real, longer-dated bonds and state-controlled companies among the most exposed. A more conservative Congress, though, could limit how far Lula could shift policy.

Texas Instruments: 3 Things to Watch Before Buying the Dividend Stock
1. Earnings recovery is real, but not risk-free
The most recent quarter backs up the idea that things are turning around. In Q2 2026, revenue jumped 23% year over year to $5.46 billion, and net income surged 53% to $1.98 billion. Operating profit also climbed 48% to $2.31 billion, pushing operating margins to about 42.3%. Strong demand from factories, data centers, and automakers drove those gains.
Cash flow got a boost too. Over the past year, Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) generated $6.53 billion in free cash flow, though that total includes $1.18 billion from CHIPS Act incentives. That's important because manufacturing investments, depreciation, and when government incentives hit the books all play a role in how much cash is left for dividends and buybacks.
2. Forward P/E: better than the past, but not a bargain
At a forward P/E of 27.55, TXN now trades higher than its forward multiples of 25.58 at the end of 2025 and 26.25 in September 2025, according to Yahoo Finance. The even higher trailing P/E of 41.43 highlights just how much last year's earnings were weighed down compared to what's expected going forward.
That forward P/E means investors are getting an earnings yield of just 3.63%, not great when you compare it to the 5.2% yield you could get from a 10-year Treasury in mid-October. And while Treasury payouts are rock solid, Texas Instruments' profits can swing with the business cycle. The company could still deliver solid returns if it keeps growing earnings and raising the dividend, but the current price gives investors less cushion if things don't go as planned.
Looking at the competition, it's easy to see why a little caution is smart. Analog Devices, for example, traded at about 23.2 times forward earnings, well below Texas Instruments' 27.55. TXN's bigger scale and wide range of analog products might explain the higher price, but to keep that edge, the company will need to deliver more than just a return to normal demand. Sustained earnings growth is a must.
3. Dividend growth meets a demanding price
In September, TI announced it was bumping its quarterly dividend up by 7% to $1.52, or $6.08 per year. Based on the October 16 share price of $276.48, that's a forward yield of about 2.2%. The company's payout ratio sits at around 85%. A comparison with other established dividend payers, such as those featured in our unstoppable dividend stocks list, also puts TXN's modest 2.2% yield into perspective.
TI's 23-year track record of raising its dividend and its growing cash flow make it appealing for income-focused investors. But with a payout ratio this high, there's not much room for earnings to slip without putting the dividend at risk. Big spending on factories and the ups and downs of industry demand are still key risks, especially if the recovery loses steam.
Texas Instruments brings real long-term strengths and a steadily rising dividend to the table, but today's valuation means it can't afford to stumble. With a forward earnings yield lower than Treasuries and a high payout ratio, the case for buying in now relies mainly on the company's ability to keep growing its profits and raising its dividend.

Texas Instruments' Sales Growth Picked Up In 2026
Texas Instruments has issued four quarterly reports since last October. Sales growth slowed in the first two periods, from 16.4% in fiscal Q2 2025 to 14.2% in fiscal Q3 2025 and 10.4% in fiscal Q4 2025. Growth then picked up in the next two quarters. Conference call at 3:30 p.m. Central time today on ti.com/ir
DALLAS (July 22, 2026) – Texas Instruments Incorporated (TI) (Nasdaq: TXN) today reported second quarter revenue of $5.46 billion, net income of $1.98 billion and earnings per share of $2.14. Earnings per share included a 5-cent benefit that was not in the company's original guidance.
Regarding the company's performance and returns to shareholders, Haviv Ilan, TI's chairman, president and CEO, made the following comments:
•"Revenue increased 13% sequentially and 23% from the same quarter a year ago with broad growth led by industrial, data center and automotive.
•"Our cash flow from operations of $8.7 billion for the trailing 12 months again underscored the strength of our business model, the quality of our product portfolio and the benefit of 300mm production. Free cash flow for the same period was $6.5 billion.
•"Over the past 12 months we invested $3.9 billion in R&D and SG&A, invested $3.3 billion in capital expenditures and returned $5.8 billion to owners.
•"TI's third quarter outlook is for revenue in the range of $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and earnings per share between $2.23 and $2.57."
